speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POWEB OP PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OB GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext: I have had no notice of such a question being asked, but there is no difficulty: in answering it. The paramount power of parliament is known to every member of this house. It is a question of honour and good faith, and successive ministers have made that clear in Great Britain for centuries. The same has been true of this parliament. When we pass legislation, however much we may desire to do so, we cannot, in theory, tie the hands of succeeding parliaments. Parliament, as the ex-Minister of Justice will agree, is free within the scope of its powers to do anything which it thinks desirable to do. But there are matters involving faith and honour and confidence and these have thus far not been disregarded either by this parliament or by the mother of parliaments.

The other day the hon.

Tobacco Combine

whether this flour had been milled in Canton, China. The answer to that is: no. The other question asked was whether it had been imported by a United States firm. The answer to that is: no. I think I owe it to the hon. member, however, to give a further statement in answer to the question. I have made, or caused to be made, very careful inquiries in order to be able to answer the question fully, and, briefly, the facts are as follows. I have the names here but I do not know that it is necessary to spread them on Hansard; I fancy that it is the facts that the hon. gentleman is interested in. A certain bakery in Vancouver which was owned and operated by a Canadian flour mill used certain quantities of this flour, supplied to it in sacks similar to the one which the hon. member presented to the house. It seems that this Canadian flour mill milled flour in western Canada out of western Canadian wheat, and exported such flour to the orient. At the request of the importer in Canton, the sacks were printed, as is common in such cases, with the name of the firm and in the language of the country of import. This practice had been going on for years. The importer in the orient discontinued the importing of this flour and the mill in question had a large number of sacks on hand. These sacks they used for the purpose of supplying flour to their own bakery in Vancouver. The flour which was contained in the sack my hon. friend had was Canadian flour, milled from Canadian wheat in a Canadian mill and supplied direct to Vancouver from the mill-not by import at all. As regards the Chinese characters on the sack, they are, I am happy to assure my hon. friend, of a very ordinary nature. On the left is ^ the name Kwong Yan Nin, Sole Representative; in the centre are the words Golden Shield, being the Chinese for the brand which was supplied; and on the right appears the name of the firm, a United States firm, Dunbar & Co. I hope that this explanation will satisfy my hon. friend.

Merchants would be ruined, apartment owners would have no more tenants, contractors could not get the necessary labour 53719-51
for their undertakings, and banks would have to close their doors. Hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house can thank heaven, that they have country folk in their midst. In the present state of civilization, there is no nation which can live aloof from the others, no country which can be prosperous by isolating itself from its neighbours by a tariff barrier. Nations are commercial and industrial collective societies for which trade is the foundation of prosperity.
Mr. LESLIE G. BELL (St. Antoine): Mr. Speaker, those of us who have followed the deliberations of the recent Imperial economic conference must have at the start taken particular interest in the world significance attached to the holding of such a conference in Canada. If we allow our minds to go back to 1930 we can recall the interest that was taken at that time in the imperial conference held in the old country, and to indicate the interest taken in the recent Ottawa conference it is only necessary for me to point out that there were present representatives of the press of practically the entire world watching its proceedings. Foreign countries especially were alarmed over the possible outcome of the conference. What was the attitude of the United States of America? It had a huge stake in the decisions of that conference. As was pointed out by some of their observers two-fifths of their foreign sales were at stake. One-fifth of those sales had previously been shipped to Canada and the other fifth distributed amongst other empire countries. But they were interested in the conference not only because of the sale of their products to Canada. The United States was further concerned in it because it had some thousands of branch industries established in this country, and it was feared by some that these industries would be called upon to supply a greater proportion of empire materials and labour. It was only natural that they should view the conference seriously because $300,000,000 of their foreign trade was involved. To mention one item alone, anthracite coal, the state of Pennsylvania supplied Canada with some $3,800,000 worth, representing one-quarter of the annual coal supply required by the Canadian people. The New York Times gave a very illuminating resume

United Kingdom
showing why the United States were particularly interested in the imperial conference. The article says:
The United States supplied Canada with 91 per cent, of all imported electrical supplies, 90 per cent of imported iron and steel products, 90 per cent of machinery imports, 99 per cent of imported automobile parts, 98 per cent of imported automobiles, 90 per cent of imported coal, 98 per cent of farm implements, 76 per cent of imported crude petroleum, 99 per cent of imported gasoline, and 98 per cent of imported raw cotton.
Many other significant percentages might be mentioned, such as the 98 per cent of coke imports which came from the United States, the 91 per cent of imported fresh vegetables, 98 per cent of imported planks and boards, 88 per cent of foreign refined sugar, 99 per cent of imported sulphur, and the 97 per cent of aluminum and bauxite.
Altogether Canada in 1930 imported products valued at $1,248,273,582, and of this amount $847,442,037 came from the United States, $189,179,738 from the United Kingdom, $63,523,966 from other British Empire countries, and $148,127,841 from all other countries combined.
To round out the picture, the value of United States exports in 1930 to other countries of the empire; Great Britain, $678,000,000; Australia, $76,000,000; South Africa, $38,000,000; New Zealand, $30,000,000; Irish Free State. $14,000,000.
The Argentine was also greatly interested in the Imperial economic conference for the simple reason that she supplied the chilled meat market of Great Britain to a great extent, and she knew that South Africa and Australia were vitally interested in this trade. The Buenos Aires, La Prensa, pointed out in a very strong editorial that the holding of the conference was one of world significance. Great Britain was such a heavy buyer of world goods that it was only natural that foreign countries should be interested in the conference, particularly in view of the desperate economic situation throughout the world.
But at the very outset of the conference a great many of these fears were dispelled. It was pointed out at the very beginning that Great Britain and the United States must come to some understanding regarding their future trade agreements, and further that there was nothing to stand in the way of negotiating trade treaties with foreign countries. At the outset of the conference a committee was appointed on Commercial Relations with foreign countries, and those who have read its report will understand that nothing was done at the conference that would stand in the way of our negotiating trade treaties with foreign countries as we have done in the past.
53719-51^
When we hear our friends opposite saying that the conference agreements are going to have the effect of diminishing our trade with the outside world, it is significant to note that Great Britain has received representations from fourteen different foreign countries seeking to negotiate trade treaties with her. At the present time she is negotiating or has given notice of her intention to negotiate treaties with the Argentine and with Scandinavian countries, and now, instead of Great Britain finding herself without weapons, she finds that the conference agreements are helping her in a great many ways. I might also mention, for instance, the holding of the Copenhagen exhibition which was recently opened by the Prince of Wales. So I think the fears of hon. gentlemen opposite are groundless.
Hon. gentlemen opposite also accuse us of deviating from our policy. May I quote the words of my leader, the Prime Minister, who, speaking at the London conference in 1930, said with regard to empire preferences:
For we believe that through the broadening of the home markets of the empire states to empire products, in preference to the products of foreign countries, every unit of this empire will benefit.
This does not mean, of course, that an attempt should be made to exclude from empire markets the goods of other countries. We must have-all of us must have-markets outside the empire. And to make these markets sure and greater, we must place no insuperable barrier in the road of reciprocal world trade. What it does mean, however, is that we should direct the present flow of trade into more permanent empire channels by preferring empire goods to those of other countries. This can only be done in one way, by creating a preference in favour of empire goodB.
May I speak of another feature? We hear a great deal from our friends opposite regarding tariffs. They seem to think that if tariffs were revised it would be a remedy for all the ills of the world. The world is a sick world today, with millions unemployed, and millions more only semi-employed. There are riots, unrest and despair. A great many of us attribute this largely to the results of the great war. Some feel that if the reparations question were settled it would be a cure of all our ills. I read a very interesting article not very long ago entitled, "This Age of Glut." The writer points out that today the present spectacle of famine and waste the world over is without record and parallel in modern civilization. Millions of peasants walk barefoot in central Europe. China's millions are driven by hunger to the verge of cannibalism. In the Argentine and the United States they are burning wheat. In Brazil thousands of bags of coffee are taken into
804	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
secluded valleys for the same purpose, or are pressed into briquettes for engine fuel, or are dumped into the sea. In Hungary and Roumania grain is fodder for the pigs. In Holland vegetables rot in immense quantites because there is no market. The cotton growers plow their crops into the soil and the rubber producers rejoice at the discovery of a new pest.
One of the great questions today is this: Can we master the problems of distribution as we have mastered those of production? Where nature produced an ear of corn we are producing a thousand. Machinery today is producing with a dozen hands what it required one thousand hands to produce in the past. The result is the very thing we aim at, leisure, or as we prefer to call it, unemployment. A very good definition of unemployment is that it is the ripe fruit of all the inventions of the last century, the object and justification of every application of science to industry and agriculture. Even the economists and scientists have been wrong, because they always figured that population could keep pace with production. That has been found to be a myth, and a new theory must be discovered. This is the age of glut, and it is no solution of the question to have hon. gentlemen opposite say that by removing tariff barriers a way will be found out of our difficulties. We must go a long way further. In addition, Mr. Speaker, we are living in the age of fear. Fear causes panics; it causes banks to crash; it causes thousands of people to lose their life savings and causes many people to take their money away from commerce and hoard it in some place where it does no good to humanity.
As I have already said, we are living in an age of unemployment. I intend to quote the latest figures in this connection, because from the speeches we have heard in this house people might think that all the unemployment in the world was within the confines of Canada. I have the latest figures from our Bureau of Statistics, and I am going to supplement those with other figures because it is very hard to arrive at anything like a correct statement of unemployment. According to our own bureau, the unemployed in the United States, from the unofficial figures given by the American Federation of Labour, number 11,400,000. In Great Britain the official figures for August last were 2,859,000. In France the figure given for last August is
263,000,	but I feel that this figure is somewhat under the actual number, and I will give additional figures in this regard. In Germany, for the same month, 5,225,000 unemployed were actually registered, while in

Italy there were 946,000. According to the figures given by the International Labour Office in Geneva, unemployment in Germany rose from 4,211,000 in June, 1931, to 6,675,307 in June of this year. In England, in spite of her tariffs and depreciated currency, unemployment figures stood at 2,821,840 in June of this year as compared with 2,577,916 a year ago. Unemployment in France rose from 51,354 in June, 1931, to 315,502 in June of this year, but these figures are far from complete and throw more light on the proportional than the actual increase. The figures for the United States are the most vague and discouraging of all and show that whereas unemployment in England increased from 22 per cent to 22-1 per cent during the second quarter of the year, unemployment in the United States increased from 23 per cent to 38 per cent during the same period. Statistics published by the economic committee of the League of Nations also show that the value of international trade today is not more than half of what it was in 1929. I am quoting these figures from the Living Age for August, 1932.
With these facts before us, along come our friends across the way and, in this so-called march of Liberalism, claim that they have a solution for all our great problems. Those of us who have studied the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite, especially their tariff policies; those who have heard them declaim in this house on the sin of having tariffs and say that we should go in for free trade-for we all recall the death knell of protection speeches-would say that this is the solution they have in mind. We have an example before us in a country that has practised free trade for a great number of years. We find that England has had to take a different course in order to save herself. The following press despatch describes in a few words the position in which the British people found themselves. This is an article dated October 28, containing the report of a speech delivered by Sir Henry Alfred MeCardie, judge of the high court, at Birmingham university. Speaking of England, he said:
"She is ringed around and beset with powerful, splendidly equipped and merciless competitors," he said. "She is fighting not for mere prosperity but for her standards of life."
"The attack upon her comes from all sides. She is in fact at war in a very real sense with the other great nations for a share in world trade and for the maintenance of her commercial prestige."
"We call it trade rivalry. In fact it is war, fought with the deadly weapons of prices, tariffs, subsidies, credits and dumping."

United Kingdom
So, Mr. Speaker, we have emerged from a war of arms into a war for self-preservation. We built our tariff walls for the protection of our own people, so that we would not be swamped by the flow of over-production in other countries. If we were to lower our tariff walls the surplus of the world would come tumbling in on us from the four comers of the earth. Prices would tumble; factories would close; farmers would join in burning their crops and in using butter for axle grease, as we have been told actually has happened; unemployment would increase very rapidly and starvation would stalk throughout the land. Should we close our eyes to such certain results? Hon. gentlemen opposite cry blue ruin; they read and quote books on economy, preach socialism, advocate the use of printing machines for the production of real money, as they call it, and urge the adoption of similar methods. I maintain that these do not constitute the policy of sane government but the madness of mis-govern-ment.
What has this conference accomplished? In the first place, it has taken the initial step in the regulation of distribution and production. It is not a question of opening up new channels of trade; today it is a question of regulating old channels. United efforts are being made to find some remedy for the situation, and it would seem that the best thing to do is to remedy our own ills first. Then, after having tasted the medicine, if it is good we can apply it to the rest of the world. This is the forward step of the conference. Some world power had to do it, and none is bigger or better equipped than the British Empire. What we want at the moment is not more trade, but stability of the trade we already have. Here was a world lesson, it was simple, it was direct. A protected market for our distribution. Production we must look after for ourselves.
That is my first point, Mr. Speaker-that the holding of this conference involved something larger than the mere sale of Saskatchewan grain. This was a conference with an outlook upon the world, seeking a remedy for the ills of the world.
Then I come to the second reason why, from an empire point of view, I am in favour of this agreement. I think the different parts of the empire met on a footing of good will, compromise and cooperation. As to what they have accomplished, the results speak for themselves; a conference sitting for one month, and making twelve different agreements, Great Britain signing seven, Canada four.
South Africa two, a conference representing this far flung empire composed of different people, different languages, and producing different products! Yet our friends opposite say nothing has been accomplished. I would like to have seen them sitting where the Prime Minister sat; I wonder if they could have accomplished half as much. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, this conference, from an empire point of view, has brought about independence of thought and action throughout the empire. It has brought Canada into the limelight of empire affairs, it has put upon us the responsibility of seeing that these agreements are fulfilled to the letter. We now enjoy the full responsibility of nationhood. Furthermore we may take a lesson in that regard from the mother country. I think we can follow in the footsteps of the mother country, which, since these agreements have been signed has shown every evidence of good faith, not only by giving notice to the Soviet republic of the termination of the trade agreement but also by postponing consideration of proposals from other countries pending the conference at Ottawa. The fact is that ever since this agreement was signed England has shown the utmost good faith. I for one will raise my voice in protest against hon. members opposite who single out any man in the mother of parliaments and say that he is trying to do harm to the empire. I understand, and I think my colleagues and hon. members opposite who are fair in this matter will understand, that no one wants to wreck the empire or harm Canada. They talk about the disintegration of the empire and seek to>
make capital out of that illusion, but let me-assure them the British Empire will survive long after every one of us in this house has-passed from the scene.
One of the good things that came out of the conference was that it produced men of empire rank. A very deliberate attack was made upon my leader, the Prime Minister. That may be the opinion of some hon. members opposite-I do not think all of them- but I am going to quote what the Ottawa Citizen, a good Liberal paper, thought of the leader of our party when he made his statement to the imperial conference in 1930. It said in an editorial:
Premier Bennett today leaped at a single bound into the front rank of empire statesmen. His speech to the Imperial conference electrified everyone who heard it. "He is Joseph Chamberlain come to life again," they said, astonished at the punch and emphasis he put behind his offer to the mother country and to all other parts of the empire of preference in Canada's markets in exchange for a like preference in
S06	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
theirs. Here were no vague phrases about flag and empire, but straight flung words that no one could misunderstand.
And after the conference was over the London Daily Express paid my leader this compliment:
-the conference has far outstripped any predecessor in actual results. The credit goes supremely to Premier Bennett, whom history will acclaim as one of the great empire builders.
We hear our friends opposite saying-always saying-that they can get no justice from the Tory party because of their high tariff principles. But one of the things that has come out of this conference is that we are pledged to appoint a non-political or an empire-approved tariff board. Any manufacturer, any farmer, anyone doing business in this land will be able to lay his case before people who are not of one political party or the other but who will grant him a non-political hearing; we are pledged to that. And the Prime Minister made it very clear that the agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada confirmed in principle the proposals made by the government of this country at the opening of the conference. On the one hand Canada retains existing preferences in the United Kingdom and secures an extension of that principle to our natural products. On the other hand Canada balances these advantages by granting such tariff concessions as will enable United Kingdom manufactures to enter Canada on a basis of fair competition with domestic industries, having regard of course to such factors as relative cost of production. This rests with the tariff board, which is to be composed of men trained in business, who will have an empire breadth of outlook and who iwill deal with tariffs in view of empire markets and to promote empire good will. And instead of my hon. friends to your extreme left, Mr. Speaker, saying that this is a wedding of high protectionists for a period of five years, it is rather the first time that those trained in the school of free trade with the world have sat around the same table with representatives of the other parts of the empire where the only safeguard was protection, and have evolved a plan of meeting each other half way.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the third part of my speech, and I will only dwell on this for a few minutes; it has been so fully covered by other members of the house that I need not devote much time to it. I only want to make this statement: From agreements such as these designed to promote the well-being of the farmer, the miner, the fishermen, and the manufacturer the most direct

and definite benefits must come to the people of Canada. I could enumerate these benefits, but I will only mention a few: free entry Into the United Kingdom market for Canadian natural products; preferences in the United Kingdom market on Canadian goods ranging from ten per cent to thirty-three and a third per cent; free entry to the markets of the United Kingdom for over one hundred manufactured commodities, including leather, fur, rubber goods, textiles, chemicals; in addition to wheat we get preferences in all the British colonies on our natural products, cheese, butter, all the products of the farm, not to mention our great product, wheat. A simple example was given by one of the Montreal newspapers the other day. A foreign ship enters a British port loaded with foreign grain. Beside it is a Canadian ship loaded with Canadian grain. On one there is six cents a bushel duty. Which is the buyer going to take? These are some of the advantages, which we as Canadians will get from these preference agreements. I am sorry that my time does not allow me to elaborate them at greater length.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), made reference to the noble words used by my right hon. leader the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), as chairman of the conference, when in closing his memorable address to this house he elucidated in the clearest manner possible the abounding success and achievements of the conference. The Prime Minister, on that occasion, quoted the words of the poet Arthur Benson:
Wider still and wider
Shall thy bounds be set.
God who made thee mighty
Make thee mightier yet.
My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), referred to these words as the marching song of the Conservative party. Let me assure him that they signify much more than that. They signify the dawn of a yesterday in the steady march of empire progress; the birth of a greater tomorrow by constructive thought and action; the recording of another milestone safely passed in the making of empire history. They were the clarion call to a greater united empire and world effort to obliterate, or at least to dispel these troublesome depressing times. They recall to my mind, Mr. Speaker, those other sentiments, so often repeated from the mouth of the Bard of Avon, whose words of wisdom have done so much to cement the bonds of our common heritage. In the play of Julius Caesar, where Brutus says to Cassius:

United Kingdom
You must note beside,
That we have tried the utmost of our friends, Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe;
There is a tide in the affairs of men
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life
Is bound in shallows and in miseries;
On such a full sea are we now afloat;
And we must take the current when it serves,
Or lose our ventures.
Shall we take opportunity at the flood, or shall we steer our course, as the opposition desire, the other way-separating our own trading ships from the empire convoy, and, trusting to fate alone, venture by an uncharted course to foreign ports? Then, for lack of vision in ourselves, lack of confidence and faith in the other great component parts of the British Commonwealth of Nations, lack of duty to our own Canadian people, finally find ourselves further engulfed, battered by foreign tariff seas, buffeted by reprisals of hurricane violence, until our ship of state, unable to endure, finds itself wrecked on the shoals of adversity-in the end, salvage for some passing foreign competing merchant ship whose ways we little know, and therefore to whose mercy we dare not trust.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasant duty for me to congratulate the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) on the interesting comments which he has just made in the house. Unfortunately I do not think, however, that he has expressed the views of the majority of the people in Montreal, of whom he and I represent a large number. I am equally pleased to congratulate my good friend, the hon. member for LTslet (Mr. Fafard) on- the splendid speech he delivered a short while ago. The hon. member for L'Islet represents a county in which have lived nine generations of my forebears and whose people pride themselves in being so well represented in the Canadian House of Commons.
After the numerous and interesting speeches delivered by hon. members within the last three weeks, I am not so conceited as to think that my contribution in this debate will throw new light on the subject matter. But as representative of one of the most important electoral divisions of this country, if not the most important, I deem it my duty to express in the house the views of my constituency which, under the circumstances, reflect -those of the great majority of the whole population of Canada.
The constituency of Maisonneuve, sir, deserves a special mention. Situated on the island of Montreal, it covers an area of about
seventy square miles and comprises a population of 116,311, according to the last census, of which 103,622 are included in the city of Montreal itself, and 12,689 on the outskirts. However, within the last year this population has considerably increased.
Its border extends for ten miles along the harbour of Montreal and I am convinced that the future development of this great national port will necessarily be carried out within the present limits of the county of Maisonneuve. More than 300 industries are established there, among which are to be found the most important enterprises of Canada, such as the Angus workshops of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Canada Car Company, the Locomotive Works, Canadian Vickers Limited, Warden King Limited, American Car Company, the St. Lawrence Sugar Company, Canadian Copper Company, Viau Biscuit Corporation, Imperial Oil Company, British American Oil, Shell Oil Company of Canada, MeColl Frontenac, Lasalle Petroleum, Du-fresne & Lock, Dufresne Construction Limited, and numerous others which it would take too much time to enumerate. More than 5,000 well-established firms do a business which include all the commodities of life. Add to this many hundreds of farmers, truck gardeners and dairy producers settled in the rural part of the county and this will give you an idea of the importance of this constituency and the interest it necessarily takes in -the present debate of the house.
I thought it proper, sir, to give these few details in connection with the county that I have -the honour of representing, so as to better explain the reason for not expressing my views before finding out what were the feelings of the great majority of my constituents as regards these trade agreements under consideration.
After all, -the people are those who will benefit or suffer from the results of these agreements, depending on whether they are advantageous or not to agriculture, trade and industry. Trade and industry does not simply comprise dealers or industrialists but also the great mass of workmen ond consumers of all kinds, without whom no trade or industry can be carried on or exist. The people being the most concerned in the results of these agreements, it is only fair that we should request their views and that ours should reflect theirs in what is best. Moreover, public opinion, or rather the good common sense of the people, when it is expressed with the truly admirable sobriety, patience and consideration of which they have given proof in the difficult conditions we are facing at

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
present is one of the best criterions upon which we can pass judgment in this respect.
It is, therefore, after consulting the people of Maisonneuve and ascertaining the views of prominent economists, public men and eminent authorities such as Sir George Paish, Lord Reading from England, Lucien Romier from France, and many others, that I have decided, sir, to repudiate these agreements as not being in keeping with wishes and needs of the Canadian people.
Do you want to know, sir, what the great majority of the people of Maisonneuve think of the Imperial conference held in Ottawa last summer and the agreements entered into? I shall, briefly, give the house these reasons, some of which are mainly responsible in deciding me to cast my vote against the resolution as submitted by the leader of the government.
This new economic regime which the government wishes to saddle on the Canadian people by enacting the agreements entered into at Ottawa, is in my opinion, the greatest political adventure ever attempted by a government. There is no doubt that it is a new policy, the Prime Minister himself informs us of this fact in the conclusion of his remarkable statement made in the house on October 12 last, and which is to be found at page 13S of Hansard:
And let those who would, for personal or party advantage, cavil at these agreements, remember that in all the history of this empire, nothing has been before achieved comparable in present benefit or in future promise to that which the Ottawa conference may claim to its lasting credit. And in the days to come, I do believe we and the generations which follow us will look back upon that conference as the beginning of a new and greater empire, bound together by common allegiance to the crown, by ties of kinship and friendship and by a common interest which our_ individual welfare bids us all strive to maintain.
What an adventure, sir, this "beginning of a new and greater empire."

speechtext:
In looking up
the French dictionary I find that the definition of this word is as follows: "bold and dangerous enterprise, which, however, may offer some allurement." Can the agreements submitted to our consideration be better qualified? This economic union of the countries of the commonwealth is an enterprise which, no doubt, offers some allurement, by grouping one quarter of the consumers of the entire world and ordering them on behalf of imperial interests, to forsake their business relations with all other nations so as to better dominate the world.
.
But what dangers lie in this conception of the British Empire! Notwithstanding the advantages, certainly appreciable in their details-for a number of citizens of the empire-and which are comprised in these agreements, they are nevertheless an open declaration of an economic war against three quarters of the world. Were we to apply them literally, it would not be long before we would witness, leagued against us, forces treble our own.
All this conscription of our wealth, trade, industries, agriculture and consumers in order to realize an impossible dream of imperial economic greatness, would but result in the ruin and disruption of the empire, as well as weakening the economic existence of each component part. Under the plea of protecting our industries and producers of all kinds against the encroachment of foreign exports, we lay ourselves open to be deprived of three-quarters of the world's markets.
I have always thought, sir, that the best means to develop the trade of a nation, both internal and external, was quality production at a price which could meet competition and extensive advertisement. The right hon. Prime Minister who had promised us, when leader of the opposition, to blast a way to the markets of the world for Canadian products would have had better success had he applied his indisputable energy and the appropriations voted for the Imperial conference, at Ottawa, he would have had more success, I said, had he spent his energy and the public money in reducing the cost of production in Canada and also in convincing the world consumers of the superiority of our products, instead of endeavouring to realize his protectionist utopia and wild dream of an ever greater empire. It is not the tariffs or restrictions or even a preference which will attract foreigners and empire citizens to purchase our goods, but curiosity and the desire which we will have ourselves created among them to appreciate and seek our goods, at the same time as maintaining the prices and the quality, permitting them to compete with other nations.

It is practical.

speechtext:
I would have a better conception of the greatness of the British Empire, were I to see all the free nations which it comprises, forming friendly relations with the other countries of the world and proclaiming everywhere the British spirit and the resourcefulness of its institutions, which have united in peace and harmony the truly wonderful association of nations of the commonwealth rather than seeing this same association isolating itself, restricting its trade

United Kingdom
relations to its members only and provoking the rest of the world to use reprisals towards it.
This is why, sir, I think that this adventure which is, in the words of the right hon. Prime Minister, "These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association"-these are the exact words consigned to Hansard, page 109-and which will have the result, according to the views expressed in the house by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), of diverting our foreign trade towards the empire, without increasing the Volume, offers too many dangers to be worth while giving it a trial, notwithstanding the allurement it may present.
Another reason which mediates against the approval of the agreements, is that it changes entirely the spirit which exists in our relations with England and the rest of the British Empire.
This reason has already been eloquently dealt with by my hon. leader and the distinguished speakers who sit on this side of this house. However, it is necessary to refer again to the situation and explain it clearly to the people of this country, so that, when the opportunity arises to appreciate the results, each can take his own responsibility for the decision he takes today.
It was Lord Reading himself who told us, the other day, at the lunch which the Prime Minister gave in his honour, to consider the spirit which animated the Ottawa conference rather than the letter of the agreements, acknowledging thereby that in the provisions themselves there is not sufficient inducement to satisfy public opinion.
In what spirit were these agreements concluded? During a whole century our forefathers have struggled to obtain for us the constitutional liberties which we now enjoy. Thanks to the spirit of initiative of our Liberal leaders and particularly the Hon. Mr. King and the Hon. Mr. Lapointe, we had assured to Canada complete political, economical and constitutional autonomy, giving it the standing of a free nation. The countries forming part not of the Empire but of the British commonwealth including the United Kingdom were no more attached to one another by ties of dependence and "common interests which our own welfare bids us to safeguard at all costs," as the Prime Minister stated, but constituting voluntarily "a free association of free nations" according to the formula adopted at the Imperial conference of 1926.
Free nations acknowledging a common sovereign, it is true, but retaining their complete freedom of action in the economic
and political spheres, in their external and internal affairs or in all order of ideas, as they think best and proper, according to the lucid definition given, the other day, by the hon. member for Quebec East.
All this is set aside by a stroke of the pen owing to the agreements concluded this summer in Ottawa, and which we are requested to ratify, without even changing a comma.
These agreements by which each dominion pledges itself not to alter its tariff policy without the consent of the others and that of the United Kingdom; these agreements on the part of the dominions and the United Kingdom to only grant one another reciprocal concessions on condition only of creating by common consent, obstacles to our foreign trade, by raising the tariff against other countries; this convention which binds us for a definite period not to negotiate any further foreign trade treaty, without the consent of Great Britain and even the other dominions, which are 'bound like us, are after all a step backward of fifty years in the constitutional evolution of our country. .
The spirit which guided the Imperial economic conference at Ottawa, as expressed in the terms of the agreements and as acknowledged in the statements of our hon. friends opposite, was to divert the foreign trade of the dominions towards the British Empire and engage the nations of the commonwealth in an economic war against the rest of the world, with the hope of making an "ever greater empire." It is a direct surrender of the principles for which our forebears fought with such ardour and the cession of our constitutional and political liberties which Great Britain herself had definitely conceded to us at the Imperial conferences of 1923 and 1926.
I should much like also, as our friends opposite, to be able to approve these agreements so as to prove to the rest of the world that the Imperial economic conference of 1932 has marked the dawn of further progress for the world and for our dear Canada ; however, we are in a dilemma, sir, which leaves us no other issue than to unequivocally and strongly repudiate these agreements.
If this conference was really a failure like that of 1930, as we contend, without doubt our duty is to repudiate these treaties in their entirety.
If, on the contrary, it has proved a success, it means that we completely endorse political and economic imperialism which all our statesmen, Liberal as well as Conservative, have opposed for the last fifty years, and

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
that all economists and wise men of the *world blame as being the main cause of the world crisis.
For my part, sir, I prefer adhering to the traditions of our policy than going backward in our history by associating my name to such a retrograde scheme.
Moreover, if we examine in detail the agreements concluded between the United Kingdom and Canada, what do we discover? Allow me, sir, to make use of a popular expression to better convey my thoughts: "Canada was done in this affair."
If anyone is to benefit from these agreements it is not Canada but England. The apparent concessions that this pact comprises, in keeping with protectionist ideas of our Prime Minister, have no other aim than of assuring the Canadian market to the products of Great Britain. The United Kingdom secured for herself, almost exclusively, the colonial markets, without granting the same advantages to Canada on the British market; it is more than time to point out that fact.

One has to realize the skilful as well as the concealed restrictions forced upon us in these agreements by British diplomacy. At times it is the price of our products which is restricted not to the cost of production, but to the whims of the world markets, such as determined by article 4 of the agreements, where our producers are obliged to offer their goods at prices not exceeding those of world markets. At other times it is the quantity and quality of our products which are limited, as in the case of ham and bacon; this restriction is to be found in article 6 of the agreements.
Articles 4 and 6 have been thoroughly threshed out and it is unnecessary to refer again to them to prove that the advantages which are offered to us with one hand are soon withdrawn with the other.
Who will decide as to the world prices? Who will judge of the quality of our products. It will certainly not be Canada. When London finds it unprofitable to purchase our wheat, copper, zinc, lead, ham, bacon, etc., it will simply enforce the restrictions included in said articles and we shall be unable to protest. However, sir, there is an article *which has not been, in my opinion, sufficiently considered. It is article 10. The latter is as amazing as it is pleasantly artless. Allow me to read it in full:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that protection by tariffs shall be afforded against United Kingdom products only to those industries which are reasonably assured of sound opportunities for success.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the previous speaker (Mr. Jean) upon his excellent address. He was bom in my native valley of St. Philippe de Nery and attended college with me. I have followed his career with great interest and I say to him that I will be pleased to tell the constituents of Maisonneuve that his maiden speech was to me a masterpiece.
The subject before us today is one of such tremendous importance that I have no apology to offer for trespassing upon the time of the house even at this late stage in the discussion. To any observer of Canadian politics, this year is one of accentuated depression in trade, industry and agriculture, of an unprecedented degree of unemployment and of an acute crisis in national finance. A deficit of more than $100,000,000 is hanging over our heads. Gur trade is languishing to a lamentable degree. Our industries, in spite of the application to an unlimited extent of this cure-all, this panacea, called high protection or superprotection, to a point which makes it very oppressive to the people, are in the grip of the depression.
Agriculture is in the doldrums. Our farmers are struggling hard to make both ends meet and they do not yet see the end of their troubles. The present government has too long made manufacturing industry the prime object of our national existence. In passing, may I remind this government that if, by tariff and taxation, it allows the greedy industrialists and financiers to impose too much on the farming communities, it will become a menace to our national security. While the farmers were snubbed at the recent Imperial conference, the well represented manufacturers were adequately taken care of. Nobody can deny that for three centuries agriculture has been the backbone of this country, but I am afraid that with the little care which is given now to this fundamental, primary industry, this backbone will be broken into pieces and the result will be a bag of bones.
This long-continued depression calls for statesmanship of the highest character. I contend that it is the duty of any public spirited man not to allow party animosity
.
to bear too much on his decisions and to apply himself assiduously to working for a solution. What have we seen during this debate? An opposition craving for information; an opposition penetratingly curious, inquisitive, and a government evasively informative. With the exception of the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), for whom I have the greatest admiration, and perhaps a few others, those from the other side of the house, even from the ministerial benches, have been masterpieces of diatribe. Probably this is good grist for the Conservative mill, but the country is expecting more substantial food from this administration. What has Canada witnessed during the past few years? A government of sane and sincere achievement displaced by one of great promises; a man of experience replaced by a man of experiment. An era of great expectation was opened, but I am afraid that before it closes, this period will be one of still greater disappointment. We were promised work and plenty. We reap unemployment increased threefold and misery in an increasing degree. Many remedies applied by the government to cure unemployment were mere palliatives which accelerated the disease. The money spent in my constituency and more particularly in my own parish, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, went into the pockets of the Tories with one or perhaps very few exceptions.

Mr. Speaker, it is now fifteen minutes to six o'clock, and, as I purpose concluding before six the few remarks I have to make, I am not making the usual request. Thereby I avoid challenging the accuracy of the clock, not to mention the veracity of authority in this chamber.
Until last evening I 'had not intended speaking in this debate but on account of some observations made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) I feel in duty bound to say something of a very brief character on the question of wheat preferences and this country's violation of the east and west statutory trade obligations in order to keep the records straight and to remind this honourable house that maritime province Atlantic seaports are part and parcel of Canadian confederation and do not intend to be starved by a continuation of the iniquitous policy of routing Canadian grain over foreign steel and through United States ports.
Time and again maritime members have placed on record the confederation commitments respecting the flow of Canadian trade over Canadian railways and through Canadian ports, and I do not purpose crowding Hansard by repeating them in this debate.

Has this house and this country forgotten the statutes of 1903 and 1904 when the Transcontinental railway project was before parliament? Written into the very constitution are the pledges that if the Transcontinental were built we would no longer have to tolerate the use of American railways or United States ports for the outlet of our grain. Those who wish may read the utterances of a great Canadian statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and examine the bond incorporated in the statutes of 1903 and 1904 and also refresh their memories by examining the pre-election pledges of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and others in the election campaigns of 1904 and 1908.
The Transcontinental railway was built at a cost to Canada of upwards of $300,000,000, constructed with low gradients and easy curvatures for the special purpose of routing Canadian trade through Canadian ports. Notwithstanding the colossal cost, the railway is not being used; the bond has been violated; the statute disregarded and the pledges unkept. I ask this honourable house whether now, under the 6 cents preference granted by Great Britain on wheat moving on an allempire route, when a golden opportunity presents itself of rectifying the wrong-in which the mother country is directing the course-we intend to sit idly by and allow American railways and American ports to continue to reap the harvest which, by every spoken and written bond and on every constitutional and patriotic ground, belongs to us.
The east and west routing of Canadian trade means much more to Canada than at first might appear. It has been conservatively estimated that as high as $20,000,000 in a single year has been paid out to American elevators, railways, railway employees, port-workers and others in the storing, transporting, handling and elevating of Canadian grain alone. What an outrage for a self-respecting people to contemplate! Think of the employment we are giving our American neighbours on this policy alone.
The hon. member for Macleod complains that there will be increased cost to the Canadian wheat grower if any change is made in the present policy of routing Canadian grain via Buffalo and New York to the motherland. I want to tell him that there is in existence today a 6 cent rate on the movement of grain from the lower lake and Georgian bay ports to Saint John and Halifax, which is a competitive rate with Buffalo to New York, and, further, I hold the view that we can secure an equally low ocean rate from Halifax and Saint John to old country ports with New York if given the business. Let the flow of

United Kingdom
grain move to Halifax and Saint John and you will find adequate ocean tonnage congregating there, anxious and willing to transport grain to the old country at as low a rate as from New York or anywhere else; in fact, they are doing that today and have been for some time past.
May I add that Canada has spent many millions of dollars in equipping Canadian ports for the special purpose of handling Canadian grain. Are these expenditures, as well as the Transcontinental railway costs to be overlooked and forgotten, as has been the railway itself, and hon. members to hold their hands up in holy horror if any change is suggested whereby Canadian ports may benefit?
It may be argued that we in Canada have not adequate elevator equipment to dispose of all of our grain in the winter months. Even if we have not, I hold that we are entitled to at least a sufficient quantity to utilize our own elevator handling and storage capacity, and if some grain must, on account of present inadequate facilities, move through New York it can be stored in elevators on the lower lake or Georgian Bay ports and consigned direct to the mother country via New York on a through bill of lading and still enjoy the preference under the present British ruling.
Empire agreements mean empire trade, empire trade means increased business to empire nations, transportation and shipping as well as others. Canada constructed at tremendous sacrifices the Transcontinental railway, and, in addition, has made huge expenditures on our ocean ports, and I maintain it is a betrayal of trust to deprive the splendid Atlantic ports of Halifax and Saint John of their constitutional right to a fair share of the grain business by handing the benefits over to Buffalo and New York. The British government, by the preference regulation, has shown the way to develop empire ports, and surely Canada, after all the betrayals of the past in this regard, will not be the first to paint the dollar sign on the union jack.

Mr. Speaker, if I were to attempt to describe this treaty in a single sentence I would say it is a futile attempt to bolster up an outworn distributive system by petty diversion of trade. Few seem to recognize the fact that one cannot divert a stream of any kind, whether it be of water or of trade, without
cost, without leakage and without waste. While I am willing to grant to hon. friends opposite every earnestness and sincerity in the matter, I wonder if they have thought of the inevitable loss of trade which will result to Canada in the transition period before that time comes, if it ever does, when full advantage can be taken of the alleged benefits under the treaty. There is little doubt that there will be waste in the transition period; even if we grant that there will be a diversion of trade, it will be accomplished at a cost which at the moment we cannot estimate but which we know will be of considerable extent.
I suggest that the release of trade from the throttling effect of tariffs is probably the most urgent need of the world at this moment outside of the settlement of our monetary problems. This applies not only to the British commonwealth, but to the whole world. The consequences of these maladjustments are difficult to estimate, but one can gain some knowledge of their effect by observing the economic disorders and the massed unemployment to be found in every part of the globe. The folly of these damaging trade restrictions and monetary policies is daily becoming more apparent. As a matter of fact, every intelligent economist of standing throughout the world has universally condemned the trade restrictions which are now throttling world trade.
The more we study this trade treaty with Great Britain the clearer it becomes that action adverse to a world expansion of trade has been taken. The achievements of the conference have been grossly exaggerated. Even hon. members to the left of you, Mr. Speaker, have at times given it an importance which in my opinion it does not deserve. Many hon. members have alleged that it was the most important thing before the country at the moment. It is not, but unemployment is, the necessity for finding remunerative markets for agricultural products is, the necessity for improving the price levels of all commodities is, the necessity for stopping borrowings on the part of the government is-these things are infinitely more important than a mere distribution or redistribution of a few commodities such as is proposed under the agreement.
What did I read before this conference had met? I read that it must not fail, that the future of the British commonwealth of nations depended upon its success, that the whole future trend of British empire evolution was resting in the hands of those who would gather at Ottawa, that failure was unthinkable, and so on, ad lib. In the light of these statements how could we expect any assertions other than those we have heard from the members of the government? They dared not

Note, all that is needed is to get the farmers of the province busy. Note also that it is one province alone that is to furnish 100,000 head of beef cattle for the British market. The ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) or anybody who knows anything about agriculture knows that it is impossible for one province alone to find a market for 100,000 head of cattle in Great Britain. Is it any wonder that Professor Corbett burst into print with some perhaps unwise but very honest statements? Professor Corbett of McGill University said:
"It was clear from the beginning that Ottawa was bound to be a failure from an economic standpoint," and that the conference had "not a chance of effecting substantial and lasting betterments of empire trade by the methods proposed."
There have been varying estimates that this treaty meant a market of from 100,000 to 400,000 head a year, and there are farmers who believed it, just as there were farmers who thought that they were going to get an
improved price for their wheat of six cents a bushel. They were to be disillusioned. There were few quite accurate comments on the conference published in the papers. The editorials were of a most confusing and misleading character. I would call them by other names, but those are the mildest terms I care to use at the moment, considering the assembly in which I am speaking. Even the Minister of Agriculture could not tolerate it; he; burst into the press with a complete denial of those estimates. He himself asserted that they were absurd and ridiculous, that there was not a tittle of foundation in them and that there was no prospect of such a market. He went further. Let hon. gentlemen opposite rise in their seats in protest if they like, but their own Minister of Agriculture is reported as saying that the natural market for Canadian cattle was the United States of America.

First of all let me ask this question: Is it fair of the Prime Minister of Canada to now get rid of responsibility for his action by saying that this policy is one for the British government to decide? Yes, I am serious in what I say. We are people who came to this country as you did; we went west, and we have contributed our toil and our lives to the advancement of Canada. Now if you say that you are going to thrust us into even greater poverty and degradation *than we now suffer, to force our grain to go through your ports, you are making a great error in judgment and in politics.
What is the meaning of this recent decision on the part of the British government? It means that from the time of freeze-up the grain will be shifted from its natural to an artificial channel, at great cost to us. Mind you, I have every sympathy with the aspirations and ambitions of those living in Nova Scotia and the maritimes generally, but let me say to them that their ambitions cannot be realized through the sacrifice of the greatest producers of natural wealth in the Dominion of Canada, the wheat growers. Their ambitions can be realized if this country will undertake to provide us with as low a freight rate to the Atlantic coast as we can now get to Atlantic ports in the United States. Therefore it means that from freeze-up onward this total volume of six hundred million bushels will have to be diverted from its natural channel, to the extent to which it goes to the United Kingdom, if it is to get this preference. In turn,

United Kingdom
this means that the chief factor in keeping down Atlantic cargo rates, that is, the New York liner traffic, will not be working for ns. Our experience in the past with traffic on the Atlantic has been that all shippers, and particularly trans-atlantic carriers, are only too eager to seize any opportunity that may present itself to advance rates. That very fact was indicated in the figures put on record last night by the hon. member for Maeleod (Mr. Coote). We find that the rate from New York to Liverpool is only 4i cents, while the rate to Glasgow, which is not a constant route on regular schedule, is 7 cents, and the rate to Antwerp is 10 cents. What the rate will be from Halifax to the old country hon. members opposite will know.
The next thing this agreement will do is provide our lake shippers association, or combine, or pool or whatever the pleasant thing is called, with an additional opportunity still further to exploit the grain growers of the west. It definitely means that we must keep our grain from Buffalo or any other storage point in the United States and that if we depart from the long and expensive channels of Canadian rail transportation we will lose any alleged advantage there may be in this preference. We must remember that we ship to the old country about one hundred million bushels of wheat, and that we ship through United States ports from one-half to two-thirds of this amount. On that portion we will now get no preference. It is easy to imagine the amount of preference we will get on the balance. What an enormous benefit this is going to be! It does not advance prices; it does not widen markets; it applies only to about fifty million bushels of a six hundred million bushel available supply. Loud cheers for the preference! That, Mr. Speaker, is what is offered agriculture, an industry which, in the tom years from 1921 to 1931- and remember that a great decline has taken place as well since 1931

has suffered a serious alteration in the ownership of land.
Let me give some figures in that connection. To-day we have 28,000 fewer full owners of farms than we had in 1921. We have an increase of 32.9 per cent in the number of tenant farmers. We have an increase of 70 per cent in the number of farms partly owned and partly operated by tenant farmers. We have a 20 per cent decline in the value of farm property which, added up, means a loss of $1,025,000,000 in the value of farm property. subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OP TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It is now three weeks
since I tabled this agreement in the house. No one will deny that the fullest possible opportunity has been afforded to every hon. member to discuss it and every detail of it including the schedules. During those three weeks many speeches have been made and much time consumed, and I am bound to say that there has been evidence of more heat than light. The opposition prior to last evening had filled some 528 columns of Hansard; the government had been content with 263, fifty of which had been taken by me in opening the agreement with the schedules. Further comments are unnecessary.
It is a strange event we have witnessed here. I venture to think in all the annals of this parliament few have been stranger. We have witnessed the betrayal of a great party, the repudiation by a party of a great policy. We have seen it forswear its leaders, forget its past and enunciate new theories entirely at variance with any heretofore held. It has sacrificed its great history and tradition-for what? I shall endeavour to show. Before I resume my seat I shall endeavour to make clear to the house just what the policy of
828	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
the Liberal party has heretofore been, just what this new departure involves, and just why it has been made.	This policy of
imperial preference or of preferential treatment of Canadian commodities in the British market was a fundamental part of the teachings of Liberalism in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In 1897 he and his minister of finance, speaking for the government, introduced into the house measures which provided for the granting freely of preferences to goods from Great Britain. What they said then was: What we give, we give freely, without compensation, without hope of any benefit. No, not without hope of benefit. True, not benefit described in words, but the latent hope that some day the British people, realizing the great concessions that Canada had granted, would give to this country in turn the benefits it had bestowed upon them. There are those who say that that is not so, and because they have made those statements during this debate, I propose to indicate very briefly, by suitable and appropriate extracts not only from their declared policies at home but from their declared policies in the centre of the empire, just what their position was.
In 1897 the Conservative party of that day, under Sir Charles Tupper, did not believe that concessions of this character should be given for nothing. They believed that if we give a preference, we should receive something for it. They believed that if we conferred benefits, we should receive benefits in return. It was open at all times for the Conservative party, indeed, their leaders had been pressed in days gone by, to grant a preference without compensation, but to that doctrine they turned their backs and said:	In this young, new country, with all its vast resources for development and the enrichment of those who come within its borders, we should not grant concessions by way of preferences unless we receive concessions in return. That was our policy; to that we have clung, and we have lived long enough to see gathered in this capital city of Canada a group of delegates from every part of the empire who have given effect to that contention of 1897.
From 1897 onward Sir Wilfrid Laurier, realizing that he had been giving something for nothing, earnestly hoped and, indeed, quietly urged that concessions should be made by Great Britain by granting preferences to Canada. His hopes, however, were not realized. I find that in the proceedings of the conference of 1902, held only a few years after we had the granting of the preferences in question by Canada, there was a memorandum presented by the President of the Board

of Trade which represented the agreed formula of all parties attending that conference in London. Listen to these words as found on page thirty-five:
As a result of the communications which have taken place, it is understood that the representatives of the colonies hereinafter mentioned are prepared to recommend to their respective parliaments preferential treatment of British goods on the following lines:
Canada. The existing preference of 33J per cent, and an additional preference on lists of selected articles-
Now, let me draw the attention of those in this house who have denied that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was prepared to establish his preference by putting a greater duty against foreign goods and lettiDg British goods come in free, to these words:
(a)	By further reducing the duties in favour of the United Kingdom.
(b)	By raising the duties against foreign imports, and
(c)	By imposing duties on certain foreign imports now on the free list.
That was the declaration in 1902 of the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and it was that very same principle that in 1930 we applied in negotiating these agreements: first of all, the free list; second, the imposition of duties on foreign goods, and, third, the placing of duties upon goods that had formerly come in free from foreign countries.
Then I turn to page thirty-seven and I find that the Canadian ministers not only were not content with that statement, but went further. They submitted a special memorandum in which they made this declaration:
While it was not deemed necessary to enter into questions as to the wisdom or unwisdom of the policy adopted by all governments in Canada, of raising the revenues chiefly from customs duties, the Canadian ministers pointed out that under that policy large industries had. grown up which had to be considered in connection with the proposed tariff changes.
I wonder what they say now, those who day after day have been talking about the recognition of the manufacturing interests of this country, to the memorandum filed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1902, when he said that any agreement entered into must have regard to the fact that we in this new country had built up great and powerful manufacturing interests. Where are they now? Where are those little minds that have been shrieking against the manufacturing interests during the last three weeks? Where are they who shrieked aloud because some prosperity, they said, had come to the manufacturing interests of this country, on every one hundred dollars of which, by the way, they pay twelve dollars to the exchequer of this country in income tax, in

United Kingdom
addition to disposition of the dividends. Here are the words of the leader of the Liberal party in 1902. Sir Wilfrid Laurier went further. He said:
Large reductions of duties had been made in recent years especially on British imports. It was feared that in some lines of importance further reductions might create a disturbance of trade which would not be conducive to the welfare of the country.
That was what was in the mind of that great leader at that particular moment, that the making of great reductions would have an effect upon business which this country dare not face. I say to this house and to the country that in the present period of world depression, such as the world never before has seen, to do just what was then suggested would bring about a dislocation of the business of this country, would mean absolute chaos and disaster. And we did not do it.
Then they desired to make clear these things. After reciting that he would not do this, he proceeds:
The Canadian ministers desired to have it understood that they took this course with the strong hope and expectation that the principle of preferential trade would be more widely accepted by the colonies, and that the mother country would at an early day apply the same principle by exempting the products of the colonies from customs duties.
There we have it. In 1902 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who launched the policy of preference without preference, who launched the policy of giving without receiving, having tried it and having realized what it meant to the development of this young country, said- here are his own words: "They desired to have it understood that they had a strong hope-" a strong hope -"that the mother country would at an early date apply the same principle by exempting the products of the colonies from customs duties." In other words, asking for free entry into the markets of the United Kingdom, free entry which in 1932 this government has been able to secure.
Then it has been said that the mere suggestion of the following of a given course constituted an interference with the policies of the mother country. Before he left this world, while he was still in the plentitude of all his power, Sir Wilfrid Laurier in this very city uged upon Mr. Hewins, the representative of Mr. Chamberlain who came here for that purpose, that this policy should be pursued, and gave his reasons for it, as I shall presently show.
But before doing that may I point out that there came another conference. Before that other conference came, having failed to make
any impression on the British people in 1902, Sir Wilfrid Laurier still desiring to secure something for Canadians, in 1905, in this very city dealt with the problem to which I have referred. I have in my hand the first volume of Apologia of an Imperialist by Mr. W. A. S. Hewins, and you will find there if you take the trouble-and I commend to every member the reading of the first chapter-the record of his conversations with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with Mr. Fielding, with Sir William Mulock, and with Mr. Paterson, all of whom, so far as I know, except Sir William Mulock, have been gathered to their fathers. Tum to page 132 and you will find the clear statement of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's opinion in 1905. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
The objection I had stated was to some extent well founded, and we should no doubt have to run some risk. It might happen that such would be the course of Canadian policy and we ought to have a policy of our own.
I asked him what would be the effect of Mr. Chamberlain's proposed two shillings preference on wheat on Canada in competition with U.S.A.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said U.S.A. was almost played out as an exporter of wheat.
That was in 1905, and we still have in the United States of America one of the greatest exporters of wheat. Mr. Hewins continues:
I quoted evidence from the United States Industrial Commission on this subject, and we discussed the price which would pay the U.S.A. farmer and exporter. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said no doubt the preference would stimulate immigration into Canada. But he said he was not afraid of U.S.A. competition; ordinary economic factors would settle that, and Canada's wheatgrowing would develop as fast as they wanted.
I said I presumed he was indifferent to the two shillings duty in these circumstances, since Canada would in any event grow wheat for the whole world
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: "Far from it; this preference is what I have been fighting for and what I want."
That is what I say to the agriculturists on the other side of the house; that is what I say to those men who have been belittling the two shillings preference. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
Far from it. This preference is what I have been fighting for and what I want.
That was bargaining. He was willing to bargain for his country. He had learned that this policy that gives everything and gets nothing did not get us very far, and so he was willing to bargain for the good of Canada and for the advancement of the interests of the dominion. Mr. Hewins proceeds :
There were Russia and Argentina to consider, which were unknown factors. He then recounted some of the incidents of the colonial conference,-
