He asked me if I knew Robson, and said he had refused to be entertained by the Eighty Club.
I said, "Well, Sir Wilfrid, suppose we give you preference, what are you prepared to give us in return?"
And I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to Sir Wilfrid Laurier's answer:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said he was quite clear and determined on the subject. He repeated emphatically his declaration of last Monday that provided he could get reciprocity from Great Britain he would fight for preference. He said he was quite clear in his own mind as to what he wanted. He wanted the wheat preference "though in the discussions this may turn out to be less important." He wanted preference for dairy produce, cheese, and bacon which he said was of "greater political importance" than the wheat preference.
I said, "Suppose we give you this, what then ?"
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: "I will give you a schedule of manufactures admitted free into Canada."
I said: "We are talking with perfect frankness and I wish to understand clearly what you mean. The preferential tariff will consist of a schedule of free goods? Will there also be included goods on which moderate duties giving the British manufactures a substantial preference are levied?"
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: "Yes; free goods, on which duties are levied against foreign countries; other goods with moderate duties, in which Great Britain has a substantial preference."
I said that if this were known in England it would affect the whole course of the movement.	,
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that the details of the arrangement must be threshed out with the commissioners and it was settled that this should be so.
And then Sir Wilfrid Laurier asked what Mr. Chamberlain would do. The matter was further discussed with Mr. Fielding, and in the ensuing conference the efforts were made, but Mr. Chamberlain passed away; the movement died; the free traders again succeeded to power, and you will recall that in the end Sir Wilfrid Laurier, wearying of the struggle that he had carried on to secure something in return for what he had given freely, found himself compelled in 1911 to abandon further efforts in that direction, and turned his eyes to Washington. There is the story-a story that cannot be denied, the story from the records themselves, the story of the policy of the Liberal party up to the day of the death of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Then came the accession to power of a Conservative administration, and in 1917 further efforts were made in an endeavour to secure the preferences which were required. We find that resolutions were adopted but,

alas, they got no further than resolutions. So the traditional policy of the Liberal party, up to the time of the accession to power in 1921, of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition, was preferential treatment for Canadian commodities in the markets of the United Kingdom. For that treatment Canada under the Liberal government was prepared to give free entry to a list of British goods while maintaining a tariff against similar goods from foreign countries, and to place a tariff on foreign goods that were then coming in free. That was the position.
Then the right hon. gentleman opposite came into power and there was, as he has so often reminded us, an economic conference that met with an imperial conference in London in 1923. Who represented this country on that occasion, before that economic conference? Canada was represented by the right hon. gentleman opposite who now leads the opposition, then the Prime Minister of Canada; by Sir Lomer Gouin, then Minister of Justice, and by Right Hon. George P. Graham, then Minister of Railways and Canals.
These gentlemen went to London and appeared before that economic conference. I sometimes think it impossible that those who sit to the left of you, Mr. Speaker, can have any understanding .or appreciation of the attitude then taken by the right hon. gentleman opposite. I wonder if they realize what was his position then. I will not leave it to conjecture or doubt; from this record I will read just what was his position, and before I conclude I shall ask why he has taken this great party from the valley of humiliation to annihilation.
Now let us go a step further. I find that the right hon. gentleman, appearing before that economic committee, which was presided over by a member of the then Conservative administration in England, closed his speech with the words which will be found at page 32 of sessional paper 35-309, volume 60, No. 7, of 1924. Let these words sink into the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite; these are the words of their leader, the then Prime Minister of Canada, who was speaking for this country:
I am afraid, Mr. President, I have taken longer than I should have. . . .
That is how the closing paragraph begins. I am bound to say, Mr. Speaker, that in the three and three-quarter hour speech by the right hon. gentleman a few days ago there is some evidence that he still suffers from the same difficulty. He proceeded:
. . . but I would like to repeat that, so far as Canada is concerned, we have come to these conferences, regarding them as conferences, with the one motive, which I know is the

United Kingdom
motive that governs others who are present, namely, that of doing what we can in the way of advancing the mutual interests of the component parts of the British Empire, believing, as X have already said, that as the strength of the whole is increased, so will become apparent the benefit to each of the parts; in other words, that the well being of the parts is bound up in the well being and unity of the whole.
Those are noble words, with which every one of us could agree. When you compare them with the diatribes to-which we have listened in this house during the last three weeks from the right hon. gentleman and his followers, you can readily understand, Mr. Speaker, why it is that the Canadian people are asking the reasons for this kaleidoscopic change. Is it a case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde? Are there two personalities, or is it wounded vanity and pride?
Now let us go a step further and see what were the resolutions that were agreed upon; for they made declarations of policy. I am going to read those declarations of policy, because they represent the considered opinion not only of the right hon. gentleman, speaking for the Dominion of Canada, but of his government, of Mr. Graham, and of all those who accompanied him on that occasion as well. The words are rather important. If you will turn with me to page 192 of these proceedings, there you will find the resolutions that were adopted. Tonight I ask hon. members of this house, sir, to listen to this resolution which was agreed to by the right hon. gentleman opposite on behalf of the Dominion of Canada. These are the words:
This Imperial economic conference, holding that, especially in present circumstances, all possible means should be taken to develop the resources of the empire and trade between the empire countries, desires to reaffirm the resolution on the subject of imperial preference passed by the imperial war conference of 1917.
So, sir, we have the Liberal party in London, in 1923, reaffirming as a cardinal principle of its faith and as part of its policy the war time resolution of 1917. What was that resolution? It will be found at the foot of page 193 of the sessional paper. Listen to these words:
The time has arrived when all possible encouragement should be given to the development of imperial resources and especially to making the empire independent of other countries in respect of food supplies, raw materials and essential industries. With these objects in view this conference expresses itself in favour of-
(1) the principle that each part of the empire, having due regard to the interests of our allies, shall give specially favourable treatment and facilities to the produce and manufactures of other parts of the empire.
(2) arrangements by which intending emigrants from the United Kingdom may be induced to settle in countries under the British flag.
Sir, I have listened with amusement to the tales that have been told and the stories that have been unfolded with regard to the efforts the right hon. gentleman has said were made to create an economic unit of the British Empire. I have looked back through the books, and I find that the resolution of 1917 was the first resolution in which, before a conference of the empire, the thought was crystallized into words. Once more, those words are:
. . . all possible encouragement should be given to the development of imperial resources and especially to making the empire independent of other countries in respect of food supplies, raw materials and essential industries.
Where are they who have been talking for the last three weeks about an economic unit? Where are they who have decried the effort to make the empire independent of other countries in respect of food supplies, raw materials and essential industries? The right hon. gentleman opposite is the author of those words, so far as the Liberal party in this country is concerned. Does he suppose that this has been forgotten by the Canadian people? Ah, sir, was I not right when I said that during the last three weeks this great party has been drawn into a position, to appease the wounded vanity and pride of their leader, that is at variance with every principle set up alike under Sir Wilfrid Laurier and under their present leader?
But, sir, it did not end there. I wonder if this house is fully aware of all the particulars of the 1923 conference. I wonder if hon. members realize that at that time the Chancellor of the Exchequer was that same Mr. Chamberlain who has been so decried here by hon. gentlemen opposite, but who at that time was eulogized by the right hon. gentleman, as I shall show in a moment. Now the set policy of the Liberal party seems to be to decry and belittle great men. Since when has that been the policy of decent Liberalism?
Now let us look at the letter which the right hon. gentleman wrote from the Ritz Hotel in London on the 23rd of October, 1923, to Sir Philip Lloyd-Graeme. Who is he? He is Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister, he has changed his name, that is all-the same Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister who lived in this city for a month or more, one of the delegates. Who was he then? He was no longer the President of the Board of Trade-that office was filled by Mr. Runciman; but what he was you all

Mr. Chamberlain had made certain definite offers-offers of a preference! Would you believe it? Offers of a preference; offers to give free entry into the markets of Great Britain to commodities from Canada. Of course every gentleman within sound of my voice will believe at once that the right hon. gentleman said: "Oh no,: we want nothing of that." But that is not what he said. Listen to his letter:
My Dear Sir Philip,-
My colleagues and I have been considering with care the proposals as to preferential duties-
Duties, mark you!
-put forward by the government of Great Britain at the meeting of the conference on October 9, and which I discussed with you in our conversations at the Board of Trade on Saturday morning.
These proposals, which it was observed were within the framework of the existing fiscal system of Great Britain, will, we believe, be received in Canada with due appreciation as of distinct value to dominion producers.
Then he proceeds:
More important are the general issues raised in the statements made by yourself in your presentation of the present proposals, and by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. I may quote from the statement made by the chancellor-
That is, by Mr. Chamberlain-and listen to these words that he quotes. These are Mr. Chamberlain's words:
"We want you to tell us whether what we have proposed is going to help you, whether our proposals can in any way be improved, and if so, in what direction. That does not bind us to accept any suggestions that you make to us, any more than you are bound to accept any suggestions we may put to you as to what we might desire by way of increasing our trade with you: but it does give us the opportunity at any rate of realizing what the position is, and then it will be for us to say whether, consistently with the interest of our own people here, we can carry out what you have suggested to us."
That involves this simple question: What were the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain? Mr. Chamberlain at the close of his speech set forth what his proposals were. He closed with words that are not easily forgotten, because they indicated his clear opinion as to what should be done. I would like to direct the attention of the house to his words, because they indicate clearly what transpired. At page 164 you will find his references to raw apples, canned salmon-"which is of particular interest to Canada"-fruit juices,

honey. They offered these concessions he said. They could not do anything with foodstuffs at that time, that is, wheat-I shall deal with that presently; they offered a preference on dried fruits, currants, preserved fruits, sugar, tobacco, raw apples, canned salmon, canned crabs and canned lobster, limes, lemons and other fruit juices. These were the proposals which the right hon. gentleman was considering when he was replying to the communication that was made by the chancellor.
Now let me proceed. This is again the letter of the present leader of the opposition, the then Prime Minister:
In response to this welcome overture I have pleasure in giving you a brief statement of our position.
Mr. Chamberlain's statement was then a "welcome overture," now it is the dead march in Saul! He proceeds:
Canada has been the pioneer in the modern development of preferential trade within the British empire. She gave us the first preference to British goods in 1897-98 and took the initiative in requesting the abrogation of treaties which stood in the way of imperial preference. This policy she has steadfastly maintained. The Canadian preference now covers, in varying degrees, practically the whole range of competitive British exports to the dominion.
Then he refers to what was granted with respect to the ten per cent discount on existing duties. But before I proceed with this I should like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite to listen to the words of their leader in 1923 in England:
Coming specifically to the proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that we state what preferential duties-
Duties!
-would be of most advantage to our producers, and noting that the chancellor quite properly observes it will be for the British government to consider whether such duties would be in the interests of the British people, I now outline some of the chief Canadian exports to Great Britain in which an effective preference would be of most value.
Preference! Duties!
The list, of course, is not exhaustive.
Wheat obviously comes first and easily foremost. It is our most important article of export; the quality is unquestioned; the market is now highly competitive; Canada's export surplus is greater than the total British import.
Next in export importance among the grains comes barley, of which Canada normally produces sixty to seventy million bushels, and exported to the United Kingdom last year about ten million bushels.
Milling, particularly of wheat flour, ranks high among Canadian industries.

United Kingdom
I ask the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) to listen to this:
It is closely and naturally connected -with our agricultural industry. The production of flour normally runs about fifteen million barrels; last year our exports reached nearly seven million five hundred thousand barrels, of which nearly five million came to the United Kingdom. The industry is capable of very great expansion if greater markets are opened. Flour is, of course, a commodity of which the production and milling capacity in Great Britain is large. The effect of a duty-
Of a duty I
-would, therefore, depend very largely upon the extent to which the Canadian miller was put in a less advantageous position than the British miller; a duty which was distinctly protectionist rather than preferential, would not, in the long run, we believe, be as advantageous to Canadian millers as the existing situation.
And this government has secured for the Canadian millers a preference of ten per cent -not ten cents a barrel-on flour from Canada entering Great Britain. In other words, a vessel laden with flour from the United States, with a cargo valued at $100,000, has to pay $10,000 before she can be warped into the wharf at Liverpool, while the Canadian cargo goes in free. The right hon. gentleman proceeds:
Of the other agricultural products, excluding those already covered, the most important are fresh fruits, apples, peaches, pears, and plums, all of which Canada produces in unexcelled quality, and, especially in apples, in very large quantities, with difficulty at present in finding profitable markets;-
Let the hon. member for Hants-Kings vote against this agreement to indicate his gratitude.
- (for Canada, a preference on fresh fruits is of much more importance than on dried or preserved fruits); cheese, butter and eggs, bacon and hams, canned vegetables. Of our fishery products, canned salmon, which is faced with competition from the United States, Japan and Russia, would at present be most helped by a preference.
But, Mr. Speaker, it did not stop there. Let us proceed:
Our forest products, with due observance of conservation principles, are capable of great expansion, notably lumber, newsprint paper, millboard and strawboard, and chemical and mechanical pulp. Canada has also large resources in ferrous and non-ferrous metals, and in the non-metallic minerals, which a substantial preference would assist in developing. Our iron and steel and other metal industries, including agricultural implements and electrical apparatus, our wood-working, rubber and other manufacturing industries would supply a wide range of products.
On a preferential duty basis, mark you! Let us proceed:
I understand it is not your desire at this stage to obtain other than a very general statement. On all the above, and any other branch of Canadian industry which might be included within the range of duties to be imposed at any time, our government would be pleased to avail itself of the opportunity, as occasion arises, of making suggestions in further outline and in detail.
Well, sir, to hear the Liberal party, after that, denounce duties is to wonder what their policy is now and in what direction they are travelling. I shall presently show that the extreme left has once again claimed them in the hope of a repetition of 1926. Thev have forgotten the great traditions and the history of their party, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is now their directing genius.
But, sir, it did not end even there. The Right Hon. George P. Graham represented Canada at the next meeting of the conference, and what did he say? Well, he said all that his leader had said and a little more too. You will find it all at pages 166, 167 and 168. I will not take up the time of the house reading it, but Mr. Graham made a statement as to the preference, which would be so desirable for Canada. He quoted, with approval, the language of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, thanked him for affording him the opportunity to speak, and then said that while we were not proceeding in a bargaining spirit-running true to form, as indicated by his leader-the change in the British fiscal system would create a new situation. Then, after referring to Canadian exports on which the preference would be most valuable, he makes a declaration of faith with respect to wheat. Listen to these words:
Wheat obviously comes first and easily foremost. It is our most important article of export: the quality is unquestioned; the market is now highly competitive; Canada's export surplus is greater than the British import.
Now mark these words:
We recognize, however, that in this case the issue has been decided. The Prime Minister has announced that tile British government does not intend to put a duty on wheat. We accept that decision. It, of course, restricts the range and value of the preference as regards the Canadian producers, but we fully and freely recognize that it is for this country to decide what is in the interests of its people and to act thereon.

Let it ring down through the ages that an ex-prime minister who had sat with these men, negotiated with them, bargained with them at an economic conference in 1923, so far forgot himself as to stand in the house and charge them with being parties to a Tory conspiracy in making agreements within the British Empire. I have

United, Kingdom
said that other reasons were put forward, so unworthy of a great occasion, so unworthy of a great agreement, so unworthy of a great bargain made between nations, so unworthy of the past of a great party, so unworthy of its traditions, that I shall leave them with that last great reason-a Tory conspiracy.
Now I pass on to something which I think is much more important in that regard. No reason has been given for this bald change of front. Was it wounded vanity and pride? Was it anger that we had succeeded where he had failed? Was it resentment that he was no longer in the spotlight, but "on the spot"? There is a striking evidence, becoming more manifest every day, that that is the real reason. Men are asking why members from constituencies that will benefit by this agreement are being led around in that way. They are asking themselves why those members-forget their duty to their country and their constituencies merely to aid and abet the right hon. gentleman in giving effect to his spleen and his wounded pride and vanity.
There is another reason. Have you observed, sir, the happenings in this house since we met? Have you observed the leadership taken of the forces opposite by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth)? He gives a reason for his position; he expresses his opinion against these agreements. Why? Because, he says, these agreements interfere with his plan. You will find it, if you will take the trouble to look, on page nine of the ordera of the day. He has a plan which he opposes to these agreements, a plan of a cooperative commonwealth modelled in government administration upon Soviet Russia. That is the plan he has. Listen to these words:
Whereas under our present economic arrangement-
And so forth.
Therefore be it resolved,-that, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately take measures looking to the setting up of a cooperative commonwealth in which all natural resources and the socially necessary machinery of production will be used in the interests of the people and not for the benefit of the few.
There again you have the model on the soviet system, your cooperative commonwealth, your soviet administration. And last night behold the sight! Day after day for three long weeks we found opposition offered to this agreement, and then last night they stood up like men and voted for this agreement with something added at the end of it! I see the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) laughs. It is no wonder. Imagine
how they looked to the left, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre saying: That is the ticket; and up they got and followed him! Cooperative commonwealth! Inflated money! The agreement plus the inflated dollar! That is all. Did you watch them as they marched up last night and voted for the inflated dollar; to bring the dollar to a parity with the pound and reduce its value to seventy-five cents? Yet listen to what the leader of their party said, not eight years ago, not nine years ago, but on the 26th of April, 1932:
With respect to the inflation of currency, may I draw attention to this further fact? It is a well known circumstance that it is very difficult to discover just what exact amount of inflation is going to serve the purpose that may be in view. Who is going to determine whether there is enough inflation? Inflation has a way of gathering momentum to itself. It is easy to step on the accelerator, but it is very hard to put on the brakes.
That was the trouble last night; they could not put on the brakes. Then the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), with her printing press, interjected this remark:
Miss Macphail: They seem to have put on the brakes now.
Mr. Mackenzie King: That is fortunate if it is in regard to inflation, because to my mind inflation certainly is one of the last cures that would be helpful in the present situation. Would inflation increase the purchasing power of anyone overseas? Would not inflation, if it is carried to the point indicated in the amendment, help very much the holding classes today as compared with others?
Then he read from Mr. Keynes. He continued :
Is that sort of thing what is desired by those who have moved the subamendment? You cannot deflate or inflate currency in such a way that it will help only those who have next to nothing, and not help in some cases those also who may possess something. Each works all around. Inflation like deflation is a two-edged sword when it comes to dealing with financial matters.
Yet last night it was: "Up guards and at 'em!" And they voted on the one hand for inflation and on the other to approve the agreement-an agreement they had opposed for three weeks-if we would only add something to it! So the swing to the left is complete. Is that why they have opposed this *agreement?

What was the purpose of the conference, Mr. Speaker? A great family gathered to secure, so far as this dominion is concerned, greater export markets for our natural and manufactured products. That is the test of the merits of the agreement, and no one who has spoken in this house has denied that the effect of this agreement will be to increase the export business of this country-not one; what is more, they cannot do it, for the figures already show that that has happened. Liberals have asked for greater export markets. Even in this debate they have done so, and now when they have the opportunity to secure greater export markets in accordance with the terms there

made, they are asked not only to vote against them but to vote not to give them even a trial. That is the answer of Liberalism to the efforts to secure greater export markets.
Let us go further. In 1923, having failed to secure them, they still continued to urge them, and they do yet continue to urge them. But, they say:	You would have had
this anyway; you would have had free entry anyway. Well, all I can say is this, and I am going to refer to this with some particularity, that if you will take the trouble to turn to pages 2384 and 2385 of Hansard of this year you will find what the right hon. leader of the opposition said on April 26. There you will find that the right hon. leader of the opposition pointed out to the house the dangers we should incur if we did not take proper steps to secure the continued benefits of free entry. Then free entry had value; why not now? Then the benefits of free entry were to be sought; why not now? Then they were not to be abandoned; why abandon them now? These are questions that thoughtful men in this country are asking. Let me read the right hon. gentleman's words:
I suppose hon. gentlemen opposite are familiar with the fact, that, while Great Britain has a twenty per cent tariff as against foreign nations-
That is hardly accurate. It should be ten per cent; it does not average twenty per cent.
-there is a provision that that tariff does not come into effect, so far as the dominions are concerned, until the fifteenth of November next. But on the fifteenth of November, unless in the meantime an arrangement has been made which is satisfactory to Great Britain, that twenty per cent tariff as matters now stand will apply against Canada as well as against foreign countries. In what position will we then be in regard to our markets in Great Britain? Great Britain has kept her bargaining power very much in reserve but it is none the less very real. She has said that nothing will take place, so far as the dominions are concerned, until the fifteenth of November, but, as I understand the provisions of the British import duties, this twenty per cent tariff will then become applicable against Canada and the other dominions, subject to any special arrangements or modifications that may be made at the Imperial conference. That is a very serious thing. Nothing could be more so.
And we secured it, and now the party opposite is going to vote against it.
Then I turn to the statement, which was wildly cheered at the time, of the hon. member for Hante-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), which will be found at page 2885 of Hansard of May 12th of this year:
The Import Duties Act provides that these preferences shall lapse on the 15th day of November as against the dominions but not as against the colonies. That, I think, is a

United Kingdom
significant fact. It is only against the dominions which -have imposed, practically all of them, protective tariffs, and in some cases very high protective tariffs, against the mother country; it is only as against these that the preferences shall lapse on November 15. It is of great importance to the ipart of Canada from which I come, and needless to say it is of great importance to Canada as a whole, that this government, at the forhcoming Imperial economic conference, should so conduct negotiations that there be an extension of these preferences past the 15th day of November.
And by article 1 of the agreement, the ratification of which is now sought and which has been opposed for three long weeks, we have secured that extension of free entry into the markets of the United Kindom. I put the case in that single sentence to the hon. member for Hants-Kings and to the right hon. leader of the opposition. There it is. We secured it. It was good in April: it was essential then; and if we had not done it, what would have happened?
Mr. Baldwin, before he came here at all, in a speeoh reported on June 17, said that unless agreement was reached at Ottawa the exemption of empire goods automatically ended on November 15, but he was hopeful that the spirit in which Britain entered the conference would be reflected by other empire governments. And we have succeeded, sir, in securing free entry for Canadian products to a market of forty million people.
In order that there may be no misapprehension as to what the real value of these preferences is, I propose, even though it may take a few moments, to place them on Hansard. These margins should be considered; no 'hon. member who votes should fail to consider them:
Butter has a fixed preference. Cheese has a fixed preference; so have eggs, milk, wheat, barley, oats, flax, rye, peas, flour, honey, condensed, powdered and evaporated milk, canned meat, meat extracts, potatoes, poultry, seeds, raw apples, beans, bran, casein, canned fruits, canned tomatoes and corn, dried fruits, preserved fruits, chemicals, ground nuts, linseed, lucerne seed, cereals and oatmeals, ketchup, macaroni, maize, chemical fertilizers, oils, sugars, tobacco.

I saw an hon. gentleman named for less. The list includes canned salmon, canned fish, cod liver oil, crayfish, whale oil, asbestos, copper, lead, magnesite, magnesium chloride and zinc, as well as leather and tanned hides and skins. All these have a fixed margin which cannot be varied for five years. All these closely and intimately touch the life of every agriculturist in this country; yet to-night, at the call of the right hon. leader of the opposition, the Liberal party is to vote no; having sought these things they now say no. I say, sir, that few more serious moments have had to be contemplated by legislators. Where is our vaunted democracy? Where are my friends opposite and to the right? After all the years of struggle we have these agreements, with the fixed margins for five years. Some are fixed for three years, and let me say that those that are fixed only for three years still have the preference, because the qualifying clause provides only for quota restrictions rather than preferences. The representatives of Great Britain said that if there should be a change and they should desire to have quotas, we would still have our preference, and at the end of three years the agreement may be revised for that purpose.
The agreement also provides something you would expect to find in an agreement between members of a family, something that is elementary in the laws touching contracts, namely, that if there are differences between the individual parties with regard to the operation of the agreement they may meet together and adjust those differences. That is what we would expect, but Still we hear bon. members opposite talk of commas, of crossing t's and dotting i's.

Now, sir, I call on this
Commons House of Parliament and the people it has sworn to serve, to witness the vote of the self-styled representatives of Liberalism. They will record their votes against this agreement. The country has the right to ask them why. Is it because the agreement stands for greater export markets? Is it because the agreement promises definite advantages to our agriculturists and industrialists? Is it because the agreement is the forerunner of more prosperous times? Is it because the agreement is the triumphant consummation of the earnest and unselfish efforts of the mother country and the dominions to make this empire of ours a greater economic power in the world, and a surer benefit to each one of us? Are these the reasons? Or is it this: that the leader of the Liberal party in this house, unable to promote the empire fiscal policy he once espoused, now turns in anger from it; that its leader, defeated in his personal ambitions, shuts out the light of reason and obdurately fastens upon those twin stars of pride and vanity? Or is it that its leadership has changed, and that under the old mantle is now found another form, the sign and symbol of a new economic and social creed, a creed that has no place in the hearts of men and women whose liberty and happiness have so long been buttressed and secured by the great free institutions of the British Empire? Is it the voice of Jacob but the hand of Esau? There must be a real reason for this default, for this betrayal of the past. For three long weeks this house has waited patiently to hear, and it has not heard it yet. In justice to Canada, in justice to this house, in justice to Liberalism itself, the reason must be made plain.
I now call on this House of Commons and the people it has sworn to serve to witness
